hints: Look at the ranges of numbers that produce encodings of the same length: 1–2, 3–6, 7–14, and so on.
What happens if you add 1 to num before writing it in binary? The leading bit identifies the length group.
You can also derive the result from the least significant side: for a positive num, its final encoded bit depends only on whether num is odd or even.
title: Encode Number Problem

notes: The encoded string may be empty when num is 0.
The encoding of num is exactly the binary representation of num + 1 with its most significant 1 bit removed.
A direct bit-by-bit construction is equivalent: emit 0 for an odd num, emit 1 for an even positive num, then replace num with (num - 1) / 2, continuing until it reaches 0.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: 23 + 1 = 24, whose binary representation is 11000. Removing the leading 1 gives 1000.
107 + 1 = 108, whose binary representation is 1101100. Removing the leading 1 gives 101100.

content.problemStatement: Given a non-negative integer `num`, return its encoding as a string. The encoding follows a sequence of binary strings: `0` maps to the empty string, `1` maps to `"0"`, `2` maps to `"1"`, `3` through `6` map to `"00"` through `"11"`, and the pattern continues with all binary strings of each length in order. Equivalently, add 1 to `num`, write the result in binary, and remove the leading `1` bit.

notes: The return value is a string containing only 0 and 1; for num = 0 the correct result is the empty string.
All arithmetic stays within the documented 10^9 input bound; standard 32-bit signed integers are sufficient for the input and intermediate num - 1 operation.
The output itself can contain Θ(log n) bits, so O(log n) output-related space is unavoidable in a string-returning interface.
The direct recurrence is equivalent to taking the binary representation of num + 1 and deleting its most significant bit.
solution.approach: The encoding groups integers by the length of their output. Adding 1 to num selects the group and makes its most significant bit the group marker; removing that leading 1 leaves exactly the required encoding. A direct construction avoids an explicit binary conversion: while num is positive, emit 0 when num is odd and 1 when num is even, then update num to (num - 1) / 2. Reverse the collected bits at the end.

better.complexity: O(log n) time and O(log n) space
better.description: Find the largest power of two not exceeding num + 1. The encoding length is the exponent of that power. Subtract the power from num + 1, convert the remainder to binary, and left-pad with zeros to the required length. This reduces the work to logarithmic in num.

optimal.complexity: O(log n) time and O(log n) space
optimal.description: Observe that the least significant encoded bit is 0 for odd num and 1 for even positive num. After removing that bit from the encoding, the remaining problem is obtained from (num - 1) / 2. Repeating this recurrence builds the answer from right to left; reversing the collected bits produces the encoding. This is exactly the same mapping as binary(num + 1) with the leading 1 removed.

bruteForce.description: Generate every encoding string in increasing length order until the target integer is reached. Length 0 represents num = 0; each length k contributes all 2^k binary strings. This mirrors the pattern but performs work proportional to the number of earlier integers and is unsuitable for large inputs.

followUps: Can you implement the same mapping using only arithmetic and bit operations, without converting to a built-in binary string?
How would you extend the idea to decode an encoded string back to the original integer?
How would the approach change if the input bound were much larger than the native integer range?
